transcript.text: Our brand new AEG FSE52407Z dishwasher keeps opening its own door a few inches near the end of the programme. Is the catch faulty? It's only 2 weeks old.

Probably not a faulty catch. This is very likely a deliberate feature. Many recent AEG dishwashers have a system called AirDry. Near the end of the programme, once washing and the final hot rinse are done, the machine releases the door itself and lets it open by around 10 cm. That lets the steam escape so the dishes dry better and use less energy. On a two-week-old machine doing exactly what you describe, that's by far the most likely explanation. A few quick checks will confirm it: 1. Look at when it opens. If it's always at the end, after the spraying has stopped, and by a similar amount each time, that's AirDry working normally.
2. Check the manual or the AEG website for your model and look for "AirDry" or "automatic door opening". If it's listed, that settles it. On many AEG models it can be switched off in the user settings if you'd rather it didn't open. The manual will show how, but drying results are usually a bit worse with it off.
3. Check whether the door latches firmly when you shut it by hand at the start of a wash. If it clicks shut, stays shut throughout the wash and only opens at the end, the catch is doing its job. When it would be a fault: - The door pops open mid-wash, with water still spraying or water on the floor.
• It won't latch shut when you close it.
• It opens when no programme is running. If any of those happen, it's a latch or door problem. As the machine is only two weeks old, that would be a warranty call to AEG rather than something to fix yourself. One small tip: while the door is ajar at the end, keep small children and pets away, as the dishes and steam will still be hot.

Thanks. It only opens in the last 10 minutes or so, every time, and it shuts and latches normally at the start. I haven't read the manual yet, so I'll have a look for AirDry. I'm a bit worried about the steam getting onto the worktop though.

That pattern fits the automatic drying feature well. It opens only in the last 10 minutes or so, every time, and latches firmly at the start. A failing catch would be more random and would usually let go mid-wash, not at the same point each cycle. I'd put this down as normal behaviour with good confidence. The manual will confirm it once you find the AirDry section. Your steam worry is a fair one, and it's a known point with this feature. 1. Check for a protective strip. Most built-in dishwashers come with an adhesive moisture-protection foil or strip to stick on the underside of the worktop, just above the door. Look under the worktop edge with a torch. If there's a shiny foil strip there, it's already protected. If not, check the installation leaflet and the bag of fittings that came with the machine. It's often included but not always fitted.
2. Think about what the worktop is made of. Laminate, stone and quartz shrug off a little steam. Solid wood, or chipboard with a cut edge, is the one to protect. If yours is wood, it's worth fitting the foil and keeping the edges oiled or sealed.
3. Keep the gap clear. The door only opens about 10 cm, so most of the steam rolls out forward and up past the worktop edge. Avoid having anything sitting right on that edge or overhanging the gap, such as cookbooks or a chopping board.
4. Switch it off if you prefer. On many AEG models AirDry can be turned off in the user settings, and the manual will show how. The trade-off is wetter dishes, especially plastics, at the end. If the door ever opens mid-wash, won't latch, or opens with no programme running, that would be a genuine fault. On a two-week-old machine that would go straight to AEG under warranty. What's your worktop made of, and can you see a foil strip under it?
I'm not sure what the worktop is made of, to be honest, and I haven't looked underneath for a foil strip yet. There are no marks on it so far, though. How would I tell what it's made of?

The easiest way is to look at the underside and edge of the worktop right above the dishwasher. That's the area the steam reaches, and it shows what the top is made of better than the surface does. Open the dishwasher door, crouch down and shine a torch up into the gap. 1. Laminate on a chipboard core. You'll see a thin coloured or patterned surface layer, about the thickness of a credit card, on top of a pale, speckled, compressed-chip board. The front edge often has a strip glued on. This is the type most at risk, because a bare cut chipboard edge can swell if it gets damp repeatedly.
2. Solid wood. It feels warm to the touch and sounds fairly solid when tapped. It's also worth protecting, and keeping oiled or sealed helps.
3. Stone or quartz (granite, quartz composite and similar). It feels cold and very hard. It's the same material all the way through with no layers, often has flecks or sparkle, and is usually thick and very heavy. A bit of steam won't bother it.
4. Solid surface or compact laminate. These are thinner, smooth, and look the same all the way through. They're generally fine with steam. While you're looking, check for a shiny foil or plastic strip stuck to the underside just above the door, as that's the moisture protection. If you can't tell either way, the kitchen fitter, the kitchen paperwork or the retailer's order will usually name the worktop material. If it does turn out to be laminate or wood with no foil strip, the strip from the dishwasher's fittings bag, or a generic self-adhesive one, is a cheap and easy fix. The door behaviour itself still looks like normal end-of-programme drying, not a catch fault.
